sections.authorBiography: Nathaniel Hawthorne was born in Salem, Massachusetts, on 4 July 1804; his ancestor John Hathorne was a judge in the Salem witch trials of 1692, a family history Hawthorne felt as a burden (he added the "w" to his name). After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 he spent years writing in near-seclusion in Salem, publishing Twice-Told Tales in 1837. He lived briefly at the utopian Brook Farm community, worked at the Salem Custom House, and achieved fame with The Scarlet Letter (1850) and The House of the Seven Gables (1851). He served as U.S. consul in Liverpool and died on 19 May 1864 in Plymouth, New Hampshire.
sections.historicalContext: Set in Padua, Italy, home to one of Europe's oldest botanical gardens (founded 1545), the story draws on Renaissance medicine and an old legend of a "poison maiden" raised on poison. Hawthorne was suspicious of scientists who treated people as experiments.

spoilerOverview.text: Beatrice has been made poisonous by her father; Giovanni finds that he too has become poisonous and offers her an antidote, but it kills her; she dies asking whether there was not more poison in his nature than in hers.

segments.script: About the author. Nathaniel Hawthorne was born in Salem, Massachusetts, on 4 July 1804; his ancestor John Hathorne was a judge in the Salem witch trials of 1692, a family history Hawthorne felt as a burden (he added the "w" to his name). After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 he spent years writing in near-seclusion in Salem, publishing Twice-Told Tales in 1837. He lived briefly at the utopian Brook Farm community, worked at the Salem Custom House, and achieved fame with The Scarlet Letter (1850) and The House of the Seven Gables (1851). He served as U.S. consul in Liverpool and died on 19 May 1864 in Plymouth, New Hampshire. The world of the book. Set in Padua, Italy, home to one of Europe's oldest botanical gardens (founded 1545), the story draws on Renaissance medicine and an old legend of a "poison maiden" raised on poison. Hawthorne was suspicious of scientists who treated people as experiments. Publication and reception. First published in the United States Magazine and Democratic Review in December 1844 under the pseudonym "M. de l'Aubépine" ("hawthorn" in French); collected in Mosses from an Old Manse (1846). Then: Admired by a small literary circle. Now: Studied as an allegory of science without morality and of love that cannot trust.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Rappaccini's Daughter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Rappaccini's Daughter: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (science and nature, love and poison, innocence) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Rappaccini's Daughter teaches about science and nature. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Nathaniel Hawthorne develops science and nature in Rappaccini's Daughter. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Nathaniel Hawthorne develops science and nature across Rappaccini's Daughter. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Rappaccini's Daughter (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of science and nature. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of science and nature in Rappaccini's Daughter. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Nathaniel Hawthorne's choices in Rappaccini's Daughter (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of science and nature, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Rappaccini's Daughter's treatment of science and nature in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on science and nature in Rappaccini's Daughter that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on science and nature in Rappaccini's Daughter. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about science and nature in Rappaccini's Daughter, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on science and nature in Rappaccini's Daughter, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
